explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. God tells Ezekiel to "…set your face toward the south, preach against it, and prophesy against the forest of the Negev." (Ezekiel 20:46) Direction AND a target. You know when your phone's map says "turn around when possible" and leaves you to figure out the rest? This is nothing like that.

Cedars sound very forest-y, I get it. But they aren't in this passage at all. God points Ezekiel south and names "…the forest of the Negev." (Ezekiel 20:46) Stick with the words on the page, baker, and you'll stay on the right trail.

Nice-sounding trees, but they never show up here. The text says Ezekiel is to "…prophesy against the forest of the Negev." (Ezekiel 20:46) That's the whole assignment. I once tried to bake without reading the recipe and ended up with a very confident mess.
A fire, yes. God says, "I am about to ignite in you a fire, and it will devour all your trees…" That's not a little campfire. My oven has one job and it's already enough heat for me.
Locusts would be a rough day, but that's not what God says here. He says, "I am about to ignite in you a fire…" Fire is the word, and the next verses keep going with it.
Water is the opposite direction, friend. God says He will "…ignite in you a fire…" and that fire will devour all the trees. No flood anywhere in these verses.

Close, but God doesn't pick favorites among the trees here. He says the fire "…will devour all your trees, both green and dry." Both, baker. Green wood usually fights back a little, and this fire isn't impressed.
Right. God says the fire "…will devour all your trees, both green and dry." Green ones don't get a pass. Both kinds are named, baker.

I know, you'd think somebody would show up with a bucket. But God says the opposite: "The blazing flame will not be quenched…" Nobody's putting this one out. No bucket brigade, no garden hose, nothing.
That's it. God says, "The blazing flame will not be quenched…" And He says it again in the next verse. Not even my fanciest oven mitts could handle this one, and I take my mitts seriously.
Yep. God says, "Then all people will see that I, the LORD, have kindled it; it will not be quenched." All people will see it, not just a few. And the One they'll see behind it is the LORD.
This one is actually true. God says, "Then all people will see that I, the LORD, have kindled it; it will not be quenched." All people, not just a few. No one will have to ask who started it.

That's what Ezekiel says they're saying: "Is he not just telling parables?" (Ezekiel 20:49) He brings it to God right after hearing about a fire that will not be quenched. I think that kind of question would sting.

That's a serious charge, but it's not what Ezekiel reports. He says, "…they are saying of me, ‘Is he not just telling parables?’…" (Ezekiel 20:49) The word he reports is parables, and the text gives nothing beyond that.
The text never says that, friend. Ezekiel tells God they are saying, "Is he not just telling parables?" (Ezekiel 20:49) That's all he reports. Let's not add words the passage didn't give us.

Yes. God says, "…set your face against Jerusalem and preach against the sanctuaries." (Ezekiel 21:2) The fire talk was about the south. Now the word turns to the city itself. Ezekiel keeps getting pointed in new directions, like a man who forgot where he parked.

Babylon doesn't appear in these verses. God tells Ezekiel to "…set your face against Jerusalem and preach against the sanctuaries." (Ezekiel 21:2) The word is aimed at Jerusalem and the land of Israel, not a faraway city.
Nineveh isn't in this passage. The word of the LORD says, "…set your face against Jerusalem and preach against the sanctuaries." (Ezekiel 21:2) Jerusalem is the name to hold on to here, baker.
His sword, yes. God says, "I am against you, and I will draw My sword from its sheath…" (Ezekiel 21:3) That's a heavy opening line. Nobody needs to wonder where He stands.
Arrows aren't mentioned. God says, "…I will draw My sword from its sheath…" (Ezekiel 21:3) Draw, sheath, sword. That's a heavy picture, and the passage keeps coming back to it.
Not a plague in this verse, friend. God says He will "…draw My sword from its sheath…" (Ezekiel 21:3) The sword is the picture He chooses, and it shows up again and again in this passage.

I can see why you'd think so, but that's not what God says. He says He will "…cut off from you both the righteous and the wicked." (Ezekiel 21:3) Both are named. It's a hard line, and the text doesn't soften it.

Right. God says He will "…cut off from you both the righteous and the wicked." (Ezekiel 21:3) The righteous are named right alongside the wicked. It's a hard verse. I think it's okay to sit quietly with it for a second.

Never. God says, "Then all flesh will know that I, the LORD, have taken My sword from its sheath, not to return it again." (Ezekiel 21:5) Not to return it again. That's about as final as a sentence gets.
"Soon" sounds hopeful, but that's not the word. God says He has taken His sword from its sheath, "…not to return it again." (Ezekiel 21:5) That settles it. It stays out.
The verse doesn't say anything like that. God says He has taken His sword from its sheath, "…not to return it again." (Ezekiel 21:5) The sword doesn't go back in, and "gladly" isn't in the sentence.

Yes. God says, "But you, son of man, groan! Groan before their eyes with a broken heart and bitter grief." (Ezekiel 21:6) Most people try to hide their feelings at work. Ezekiel gets told to do the opposite, in public.

explanations.answer: Shave his head with a sword
explanations.explanation: No shaving in this passage, friend. God tells Ezekiel, "…groan! Groan before their eyes with a broken heart and bitter grief." (Ezekiel 21:6) The assignment is groaning, and everyone gets to watch.
No digging here. God says, "Groan before their eyes with a broken heart and bitter grief." (Ezekiel 21:6) That's the job: groaning where people can see. No tools needed, just a heavy heart.

explanations.answer: Because of the news that is coming
explanations.explanation: That's the answer. When the people ask why he's groaning, Ezekiel is to say, "Because of the news that is coming." (Ezekiel 21:7) He doesn't give the details in that line. It makes you want to ask what news, doesn't it?

explanations.answer: Because his own home has been lost
explanations.explanation: That's not what he's told to say. The line is, "Because of the news that is coming." (Ezekiel 21:7) The groaning is about what's on its way, and the text gives no reason beyond that.

explanations.answer: Because the elders would not listen
explanations.explanation: Not here, baker. When the people ask why he's groaning, Ezekiel is to answer, "Because of the news that is coming." (Ezekiel 21:7) That's the only reason given in these verses.

True. Ezekiel says, "Every heart will melt, and every hand will go limp. Every spirit will faint, and every knee will turn to water." (Ezekiel 21:7) Knees are the part that's supposed to hold you up. When they turn to water, you're not holding anything up.

This one is actually true. Ezekiel says, "Every spirit will faint, and every knee will turn to water." (Ezekiel 21:7) Every knee, not a few. I think that's a heavy picture, because knees are what hold a person up.

I see where you're going, but no party here. God says, "…it is sharpened for the slaughter, polished to flash like lightning!" (Ezekiel 21:10) This sword has a serious job, and it isn't for a celebration. It's a heavy one.

Right. God says the sword is "…sharpened for the slaughter, polished to flash like lightning!" (Ezekiel 21:10) Nothing about it is for a celebration. It's a heavy part of the passage, and I'll say so plainly.

A shiny sword on a wall would be a nice decoration, but that's not the plan. God says it is "…appointed to be polished, to be grasped in the hand." (Ezekiel 21:11) This sword is meant to be picked up and used.

That's it. The verse says the sword is "appointed to be polished, to be grasped in the hand… to be placed in the hand of the slayer." (Ezekiel 21:11) No wall, no display. It's polished to be picked up.

Yes. God says, "…the sword is wielded against My people; it is against all the princes of Israel!" (Ezekiel 21:12) The princes of Israel are named right along with His people. That's why Ezekiel is told to cry out and wail.
Egypt isn't named here. God says, "…the sword is wielded against My people; it is against all the princes of Israel!" (Ezekiel 21:12) It's close to home, and that's why Ezekiel is told to wail.

Babylon and its kings aren't mentioned in this verse. God says, "…the sword is wielded against My people; it is against all the princes of Israel!" (Ezekiel 21:12) The people and the princes of Israel are the ones named.
Yes. God calls it "…a sword that slays, a sword of great slaughter closing in on every side!" (Ezekiel 21:14) Every side is the phrase the verse uses. I think that's a hard picture to sit with.
The verse doesn't say that. It calls the sword "…a sword of great slaughter closing in on every side!" (Ezekiel 21:14) Closing in on every side is the picture the text gives.
No hiding in this verse, friend. God calls it "…a sword of great slaughter closing in on every side!" (Ezekiel 21:14) Nothing about nighttime, and nothing about waiting around.

Stumble. God says, "So that their hearts may melt and many may stumble, I have appointed at all their gates a sword for slaughter." (Ezekiel 21:15) The sword is appointed at all their gates, so that hearts melt and many stumble. It's a hard verse, and it doesn't hide that.

Rejoicing doesn't fit this verse. God says the sword is appointed "So that their hearts may melt and many may stumble…" (Ezekiel 21:15) Melting hearts and stumbling people. There isn't any party at these gates.
Resting isn't in this verse, baker. The sword is appointed "So that their hearts may melt and many may stumble…" (Ezekiel 21:15) Stumble is the word the verse uses.

Yes. The message says, "Slash to the right; set your blade to the left—wherever your blade is directed." (Ezekiel 21:16) Both directions are named in the verse. Right, then left, wherever the blade is directed.
East isn't in this verse. It says, "Slash to the right; set your blade to the left—wherever your blade is directed." (Ezekiel 21:16) Right and left are the two directions named.

Back in the sheath is exactly what we're told won't happen. God said earlier He took it out "…not to return it again." (Ezekiel 21:5) And this verse says to set the blade to the left. The sword stays out.

That's it. God told Ezekiel, "…prophesy and strike your hands together." (Ezekiel 21:14) and then at the end says, "I too will strike My hands together…" (Ezekiel 21:17) Ezekiel's hands clapping together match what God says He will do. That's a quiet link to catch.

Ezekiel is told to strike his thigh (Ezekiel 21:12), but God doesn't say He'll do that. At the end He says, "I too will strike My hands together…" (Ezekiel 21:17) Hands, not thigh. Close, but a different motion.

That one is Ezekiel's job: "Cry out and wail, O son of man…" (Ezekiel 21:12) What God says He will do is different: "I too will strike My hands together…" (Ezekiel 21:17) Same hands Ezekiel was told to use.

True. God says, "I too will strike My hands together, and I will satisfy My wrath." (Ezekiel 21:17) Then comes the last line: "I, the LORD, have spoken." That's a serious ending, and the text leaves it plain.

This one is actually true. God says, "I too will strike My hands together, and I will satisfy My wrath." (Ezekiel 21:17) And right after that, the message closes with "I, the LORD, have spoken." It's the last thing before the end.
